questions.question: A scientist compares two different series circuits. Circuit A uses a 9V battery and Circuit B uses a 1.5V battery. Both circuits are otherwise identical. Why does Circuit A have a larger current flowing through it?
options: The 9V battery is physically larger and contains more total electrons to release into the circuit.
The 9V battery has a stronger ability to 'push' the existing electric charges through the circuit.
The 9V battery reduces the overall resistance of the wires to allow easier flow.
The 9V battery creates a stronger electrostatic attraction that pulls protons toward its negative terminal.

questions.question: In a series circuit, a 12V battery is connected to three bulbs. The voltage across Bulb A is measured as 5V, and the voltage across Bulb B is 4V. What is the voltage across Bulb C?
options: 12V, because each component in a series circuit receives the full battery voltage.
3V, because the voltages across the components must add up to the battery voltage.
9V, because the voltage across Bulb C is the sum of the voltages of Bulbs A and B.
1.5V, because the voltage is halved for each subsequent component in the loop.

questions.question: A student connects three 1.5V cells in series to make a battery. What is the total voltage of this battery, and why?
options: 1.5V, because the voltage of a battery in series is equal to the voltage of a single cell.
4.5V, because the total voltage of cells in series is the sum of the individual cell voltages.
3.0V, because the total voltage is calculated by averaging the cell voltages.
0.5V, because the voltage of each cell is divided by the total number of cells in the circuit.

questions.question: When a battery is connected to a complete series circuit, how do the electrons behave within the conducting wires?
options: They vibrate back and forth around fixed positions without making any net progress through the loop.
They are pushed in a single, continuous direction all the way around the circuit loop.
They flow from both terminals of the battery simultaneously and meet in the middle of the circuit.
They alternate their direction of travel every few seconds as the battery's chemical charges swap sides.

questions.question: A student states: 'Before we close the switch to turn on a circuit, the copper wires inside contain absolutely no electric charge.' Why is this statement incorrect?
options: The copper wires are already fully charged with static electricity from being handled by the student.
The atoms making up the copper wires naturally contain positive and negative electric charges at all times.
The battery constantly leaks electric charges into the wires even when the switch is open.
Air molecules surrounding the open circuit continuously deposit charges onto the wire's surface.

questions.question: A very long series circuit spans several meters across a classroom. When the switch is closed, a bulb at the far end lights up almost instantly. What explains this immediate response?
options: The chemical reaction inside the battery increases its voltage instantaneously to push air through the circuit.
Electrons everywhere in the circuit start moving at the same time as soon as the circuit is complete.
A single electron travels from the battery to the far bulb at the speed of light.
The closing of the switch creates a physical vacuum that sucks the electrons instantly to the other side.

questions.question: While the electrical signal in a circuit travels extremely fast, the actual physical movement of individual electrons through the wire is characterized by which of the following?
options: They zip along at nearly the speed of light.
They move very slowly, at a speed of just a few millimeters per second.
They do not move along the wire at all; only energy waves pass through them.
They travel at the speed of sound through the solid metal.

questions.question: A technician is examining a faulty filament bulb that prevents a series circuit from working. What is the physical reason why current cannot flow through this bulb?
options: The glass bulb has cracked, allowing air to increase the electric charge of the filament.
The filament is broken, which creates a physical gap in the circuit path that the current cannot cross.
The metal screw thread has become magnetized, which repels the incoming electrons.
The filament has melted together into a thick block, preventing the voltage from pushing through it.

questions.question: A series circuit contains a battery, a switch, a working motor, and a faulty buzzer that has an internal break. The motor does not run. How can a technician get the motor to run without removing the faulty buzzer or adding another power source?
options: Connect a wire from one terminal of the buzzer to the other terminal to bypass it.
Place a second switch in series next to the faulty buzzer.
Reverse the connections of the battery to push the current backward through the buzzer.
Open the switch to allow static charge to build up on the buzzer's casing.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the physical pathway of a series circuit?
options: It contains multiple independent loops, allowing current to choose different paths.
It is an electric circuit with exactly one complete loop from one end of a battery to the other.
It is a network of wires where components are connected to ground at multiple points.
It is a circuit where every component is connected to its own separate power cell.

questions.question: Why is an ideal ammeter designed so that it can measure the current flowing through it without affecting the overall current in the circuit?
options: It has a very high voltage that pushes the current faster to compensate for its presence.
It is designed to have no significant effect on the flow of current in the circuit it is connected into.
It absorbs all the electrons and replaces them with fresh ones from its internal battery.
It temporarily converts the electric current into static electricity to measure it.

questions.question: A series circuit contains a battery, an ammeter, and two different bulbs (Bulb X and Bulb Y). Bulb X is much brighter than Bulb Y. If the ammeter measures 0.4 A before Bulb X, what will the current be at a point between Bulb X and Bulb Y?
options: Less than 0.4 A, because Bulb X uses up some of the current to produce light.
Exactly 0.4 A, because the current in a series circuit is the same everywhere.
More than 0.4 A, because the current must speed up to reach the dimmer Bulb Y.
0.2 A, because the current is shared equally between the two bulbs.

questions.question: A series circuit consists of a battery and a single bulb. A student adds a second bulb in series with the first one. What happens to the current in the circuit?
options: The current decreases only in the wire after the second bulb, while remaining high before it.
The current remains exactly the same everywhere because the battery's voltage is unchanged.
The current changes everywhere in the circuit, on both sides of the new component.
The current increases everywhere because there are now more components to pull charge.

questions.question: A student wants to measure the voltage across a resistor in a series circuit. How should they connect the voltmeter?
options: Disconnect one wire from the resistor and insert the voltmeter in series in that gap.
Connect the voltmeter's terminals directly across the terminals of the resistor, in parallel with it.
Wrap the voltmeter's wires around the battery casing without touching the circuit wires.
Connect one terminal of the voltmeter to the resistor and the other to a metal water pipe.

questions.question: A plastic rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes statically charged. When held near some tiny pieces of paper (which contain electric charges), the paper pieces jump toward the rod. What does this demonstrate?
options: Charged objects can only exert forces on metals that conduct electricity.
Objects with a static electric charge can exert a force on other objects that contain electric charge.
Static electricity physically turns non-magnetic materials into permanent magnets.
The rod must touch the paper pieces to transfer the charges before any force can exist.

questions.question: Two suspended balloons are given electric charges. Balloon A is given a positive charge, and Balloon B is given a negative charge. If they are brought close to each other without touching, what will be observed?
options: They will push away from each other because their charges are different.
They will attract each other because objects with opposite electric charges attract.
Nothing will happen because electrostatic forces require direct physical contact.
They will both lose their charges instantly and fall straight down.

questions.question: A student rubs two identical plastic rulers with the same woollen cloth, giving both rulers a negative charge. If the student brings the charged ends of the two rulers near each other, what will happen?
options: They will repel each other because objects with the same electric charge repel each other.
They will attract each other because they are made of the same material.
They will neutralize each other and spark because their charges are identical.
They will show no interaction because static charges only affect unlike materials.

questions.question: Inside the atoms of a copper wire, there are particles with positive charges and particles with negative charges. What are the negatively charged particles called?
options: Protons
Neutrons
Electrons
Nuclei

questions.question: When a plastic rod is rubbed with a woollen cloth, the rod becomes negatively charged. What is the fundamental cause of this charging process?
options: Positively charged protons are rubbed off the rod and onto the cloth.
Electrons are transferred from one object to another, depending on the materials they are made of.
The friction creates new negative charges that did not exist inside the atoms before.
Magnetic forces within the cloth convert neutral atoms into electrons.

questions.question: Why is it very difficult to build up a static electric charge on an iron rod by rubbing it while holding it in your bare hand?
options: Iron atoms do not contain any electrons that can be transferred.
Metals are conductors, so the electric charge easily flows through them and prevents a charge from building up.
Iron has an extremely rough surface that destroys electrostatic charges as they form.
Metals repel all electrostatic forces, making them completely immune to charge transfer.
